author: EmuCore - Hub
title: Use frame skipping only as a PS2 performance diagnostic
summary: Run a brief A/B test to learn whether reducing presented frames changes emulation speed, input, audio, and scene timing, then restore the original value instead of treating visual discontinuity as a universal performance fix.
heroAlt: PCSX2 frame-rate display comparison illustrating how presentation changes must be measured carefully

sourceLabels.android-frame-pacing: Frame pacing and display cadence concepts

blocks.text: Measure simulation speed separately from displayed smoothness

Frame skipping can reduce presentation work or change cadence, but it may not reduce the emulated CPU workload that makes a PS2 scene slow. It can also create uneven motion, harm timing-sensitive input, and make a counter look better without restoring game speed. Use it for one short controlled branch: compare emulator speed, frame time, audio, and a repeatable input sequence before deciding what subsystem to investigate next.
Do not save over critical progress or judge rhythm, racing, or fighting-game timing while frame skipping is active. The diagnostic output may be visibly discontinuous by design.

items: A normal save before a repeatable slow scene.
Baseline frame skipping disabled and all speed controls at normal values.
Emulation-speed, frame-time, and audio observations recorded together.
A short input sequence with a visible response landmark.
Stable device temperature and matched cache state.
1. Cold-boot the scene with frame skipping disabled and record the baseline route.
2. Mark emulator speed, frame-time behavior, audio cadence, and input response.
3. Enable the smallest available frame-skip diagnostic value without changing speed controls.
4. Replay the identical route for no longer than needed to observe the effect.
5. Determine whether emulation speed improves or only displayed motion changes.
6. Check whether audio remains synchronized and the input landmark occurs at the same game time.
7. Disable frame skipping and repeat the baseline to confirm recovery.
8. Use the response to guide CPU, GPU, pacing, or thermal diagnosis rather than keeping the setting by default.

blocks.text: If skipping presentation work improves emulation speed substantially, the scene may be sensitive to rendering or display cost. If speed remains low while motion becomes choppier, the limiting work likely remains elsewhere. Mixed results can occur when power budgets are coupled, so the final baseline confirmation is essential.
The test is complete only after the original presentation path is restored and the result distinguishes speed from appearance.

items: The same scene and input route are used in both branches.
Emulation speed and audio are recorded, not FPS alone.
Only the frame-skip value changes.
The baseline returns after the option is disabled.
No timing-sensitive progress is saved during the test.
A speed limiter or fast-forward changes too: reset controls and repeat.
The second route is thermally slower: cool and restart.
Only a menu animation is compared: use actual gameplay.
The title internally changes camera or load: choose a fixed checkpoint.

blocks.text: Set frame skipping to disabled, restore the recorded speed and synchronization controls, cold-boot the title, and confirm normal audio and input timing. Keep only the classification notes and send persistent slowdowns to the matching diagnostic workflow.
Frame skipping is not the same as a lower game frame rate

A PS2 title may intentionally update at 30 frames per second while the emulator presents on a different cadence. Skipping emulator output can discard presentation work; it does not rewrite the game's simulation design or guarantee correct pacing on the Android display.
